subject: Pathology
vignette: A 62-year-old man in Japan presents with progressive nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and unilateral hearing loss. Examination reveals a mass in the nasopharynx, and there is no evidence of distant lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows a lymphoepithelial carcinoma with sheets of malignant epithelial cells surrounded by lymphocytes. Serology is positive for antibodies to a herpesvirus.
question: Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation_correct: Epstein-Barr virus is strongly associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which is endemic in southern China and Southeast Asia and classically presents as a lymphoepithelial mass. EBV is also associated with Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and primary CNS lymphoma in immunocompromised patients. The dense lymphoid infiltrate in the biopsy is characteristic of EBV-driven carcinomas.

explanation_incorrect.B: Hepatitis C virus drives hepatocellular carcinoma and is linked to lymphoproliferative disorders, but it has no role in nasopharyngeal tumors.
explanation_incorrect.D: Human herpesvirus 8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, and also primary effusion lymphoma and multicentric Castleman disease, not nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a malignancy of CD4-positive T cells that does not form nasopharyngeal masses.
explanation_incorrect.C: Human papillomavirus types 16 and 18 cause cervical carcinoma and also head and neck (oropharyngeal) cancer, but the nasopharynx is not a site associated with HPV.

educationalObjective: Epstein-Barr virus causes nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and primary CNS lymphoma in immunocompromised patients.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 45-year-old woman from Egypt presents with intermittent painless gross hematuria and dysuria. She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections, and urine studies reveal schistosome eggs with a terminal spine, and serology for Schistosoma haematobium is positive. Urinary tract imaging shows an irregular mass in the bladder wall.
question: Which of the following tumor types is most likely to arise from this chronic infection?

options.text: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the bladder
Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder

explanation_correct: Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection of the urinary bladder causes chronic inflammation and squamous metaplasia, which in turn leads to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. This contrasts with the developed world, where bladder cancer is predominantly urothelial and driven by cigarette smoke and aromatic amines. Schistosoma haematobium is also associated with bladder stones and obstructive uropathy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Urothelial carcinoma is the usual bladder tumor where schistosomiasis is absent, and it is classically linked to smoking and aromatic amine exposure rather than to parasitic infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholangiocarcinoma follows chronic infection or infestation of the biliary tree, classically by the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis, not by a bladder schistosome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises in the setting of chronic hepatitis B or C or aflatoxin exposure, and the schistosome that causes hepatic portal fibrosis (S. mansoni) is not the biliary carcinogen described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with Helicobacter pylori infection and with nitrosamine exposure, not with Schistosoma haematobium.

educationalObjective: Schistosoma haematobium infection of the bladder causes squamous cell carcinoma; Clonorchis sinensis causes cholangiocarcinoma.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with a 20-year history of gastroesophageal reflux presents with dyspepsia and early satiety. Upper endoscopy reveals a gastric ulcerating mass in the antrum, and biopsies show intestinal-type adenocarcinoma with abundant gland formation. Gastric biopsy also demonstrates numerous organisms colonizing the antral mucosa with associated chronic active gastritis. He later develops a distinct dense lymphoid infiltrate of the stomach that is monoclonal.
question: Which of the following pairs of malignancies is most closely linked to the organism found on biopsy?

options.text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and Kaposi sarcoma
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix

explanation_correct: Helicobacter pylori is associated with both gastric adenocarcinoma (particularly the intestinal type) and gastric MALT lymphoma, a low-grade B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. The lymphoma can regress with eradication of the organism, which is a favorite Step 1 teaching point. H. pylori drives chronic inflammation, atrophic gastritis, and intestinal metaplasia that set the stage for carcinoma.

explanation_incorrect.C: Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma are both EBV-related, and neither arises from gastric Helicobacter infection.
explanation_incorrect.D: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and cervical carcinoma are associated with tobacco and alcohol (esophagus) and HPV (cervix), not H. pylori.
explanation_incorrect.A: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is HTLV-1 driven, and Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 driven, with neither organism colonizing the stomach mucosa in this pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cholangiocarcinoma is linked to the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis, and hepatocellular carcinoma to hepatitis B and C, not to H. pylori.

educationalObjective: Helicobacter pylori is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT lymphoma.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 34-year-old woman from the Caribbean presents with a rapidly enlarging, violaceous plaque on her lower leg and similar lesions on the oral mucosa. She has been on immunosuppressive therapy since a kidney transplant 4 years ago. Biopsy shows a spindle cell proliferation forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated erythrocytes.
question: Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for this lesion?
explanation_correct: Human herpesvirus 8 (Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus) causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumor that produces violaceous cutaneous plaques and is strongly favored by immunosuppression, particularly in transplant recipients and people with HIV. The spindle cells form slit-like spaces containing red cells, which is the histologic signature. HHV-8 is also associated with primary effusion lymphoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Epstein-Barr virus causes Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and primary CNS lymphoma in immunocompromised patients, but not this vascular spindle cell tumor.
explanation_incorrect.B: Human papillomavirus type 18 is a mucosal oncogenotype causing cervical and anal carcinomas through E6 and E7 inactivation of p53 and Rb.
explanation_incorrect.D: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, with lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia, not violaceous vascular plaques.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hepatitis B virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and can trigger membranous nephropathy, but it does not produce vascular tumors of skin.

educationalObjective: Human herpesvirus 8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, especially in immunosuppressed patients.
